title: Noble Fir Nativity
subject: Contracts
subtopic: Supervening impracticability / illegality (mistake as alternative theory)
stem:
Mary chairs the Living Nativity committee at a church in California and on May 20 wrote to several wholesale evergreen nurseries asking about 100 noble firs for the church's annual outdoor Nativity scene. On June 1, she received the following signed letter from a wholesale tree farm in Oregon run by Paul:

"We have just obtained 100 of the noble firs you inquired about and can supply them for $180 each. We can guarantee shipment no later than August 1."

On June 10, Paul sold and delivered the same firs to another church for $215 each. Unaware of that transaction, Mary on the morning of June 11 mailed Paul a letter rejecting the offer, but, changing her mind an hour later, retrieved from her local post office the letter of rejection and immediately dispatched to Paul a letter of acceptance, which Paul received on June 14. On June 9, a valid federal Plant Protection Act quarantine order making the interstate shipment of noble firs from Oregon punishable as a federal crime had become effective, but neither Mary nor Paul was aware until June 15 that the quarantine was already in effect.

As between Mary and Paul, which of the following is an accurate statement?
call: As between Mary and Paul, which of the following is an accurate statement?

choices.A: If a contract was formed, it is voidable because of mutual mistake.
choices.B: No contract was formed, because Mary's June 11 rejection was effective on dispatch.
choices.C: No contract was formed, because Paul's June 10 sale of the firs to another merchant revoked the offer to Mary.
choices.D: If a contract was formed, it is unenforceable because of supervening impracticability.

rightExplanation:
A contract was likely formed. The June 10 sale to another church, standing alone, is not an effective revocation — revocation of an offer requires that the offeree receive notice of the revocation before accepting, and mere resale does not give notice. The June 11 morning rejection was never received (Mary retrieved it from her post office the same hour and replaced it with an acceptance that Paul received on June 14); under the mailbox rule, an acceptance is effective on dispatch, and a rejection — unlike an acceptance — is effective only on receipt, so the attempted rejection never terminated the offer. By the time Paul received the acceptance, no rejection had reached him and no notice of revocation had been given.

The contract, once formed, is voidable because of mutual mistake. Both Mary and Paul mistakenly believed the contract was lawful. The legality of the sale was a basic assumption on which the contract rested, and the mistake goes to the very heart of the bargain. Gold Key: a supervening criminal statute that makes performance illegal supports BOTH mutual mistake (Restatement § 152) and supervening impracticability (Restatement § 261); the original NCBE key uses mutual mistake as the framed answer, and the official scoring note acknowledged that impracticability (answer D) was also credited.

c3.label: C (revocation by resale)
c3.text: is cut on the notice element. Restatement § 50(1) requires receipt of revocation; resale to a third party is not notice to the original offeree. Visible from the stem: Mary is described as "unaware of that transaction" when she dispatched the acceptance. The choice is NOT_TRUE for misstating the rule (it presents resale alone as a complete revocation without the notice element).

c3.label: B (rejection effective on dispatch)
c3.text: is cut on the asymmetry between acceptance and rejection. The mailbox rule applies to acceptance, not rejection. Visible from the stem: Mary retrieved the rejection letter from her local post office the same hour and replaced it with an acceptance, so the rejection never reached Paul. The choice is NOT_RESPONSIVE for asserting a formation rule (mailbox rule on dispatch) that does not apply to the fact it cites (rejection).

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: A and D survive to the final axis: mutual mistake versus supervening impracticability. Both are doctrinally defensible on the same facts. The single axis they fight on is which discharge theory the NCBE's framed key picks when a federal criminal statute takes effect mid-transaction.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: The Gold Key resolves the axis: when a supervening criminal statute triggers, BOTH mutual mistake (Restatement § 152) and supervening impracticability (Restatement § 261) may discharge the contract; the original NCBE key uses mutual mistake, with the official scoring note acknowledging that supervening impracticability was also credited. Apply the NCBE framing → A. A student without the Gold Key is in anchor_gap territory; the trap is the dominant-trap attractiveness of D, not a structural cut.

studentScript: Step 1: Was a contract formed? The June 10 resale is not a revocation (Mary had no notice). The June 11 morning rejection was retrieved the same hour and never reached Paul. The acceptance was dispatched the same hour, before any rejection or revocation reached Paul, and the mailbox rule makes acceptance effective on dispatch. Contract formed. Step 2: Is it enforceable? The federal PPA quarantine on June 9 made performance illegal, unknown to both. Two discharge theories apply. The NCBE framed key is mutual mistake. Silver Key: mailbox rule is for acceptance, not rejection. Gold Key: supervening criminal statute triggers BOTH mistake and impracticability; pick the NCBE framed key. Choose A.

A.signal: After the formation distractors are cut and the impracticability-vs-mistake axis is named, the Gold Key resolves to the NCBE's framed key.
A.lawyer: Mutual mistake of a basic assumption (legality of the sale) makes the contract voidable. Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 152.

B.signal: The mailbox rule governs acceptance (dispatch), not rejection (receipt). Mary retrieved the rejection the same hour, so the rejection never reached Paul.
B.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 38 (rejection effective on receipt) and § 63 (mailbox rule for acceptance). The rejection never terminated Mary's power of acceptance.

C.signal: Revocation of an offer requires receipt of notice by the offeree. The resale to a third party is not, by itself, notice to Mary.
C.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 50(1): revocation is effective only when the offeree receives it. Indirect revocation by resale to a third party requires that the offeree learn of it before accepting.

D.signal: This is the dominant trap. The federal PPA quarantine does make performance illegal, but the NCBE's framed key is mutual mistake; the Gold Key resolves the axis.
D.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 261 (discharge by supervening impracticability) and § 264 (existing impracticability). The NCBE scoring note for QID 14391 acknowledged that this answer was also credited.

goldKeys.statement: A supervening criminal statute that makes performance illegal supports BOTH mutual mistake (Restatement § 152) and supervening impracticability (Restatement § 261); the original NCBE key uses mutual mistake as the framed answer, with impracticability also credited.
goldKeys.trigger: federal criminal statute takes effect mid-transaction, both parties unaware
goldKeys.unlocks: dominant-trap discrimination between A (mistake) and D (impracticability) on supervening-illegality facts
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 152, 261; Plant Protection Act, 7 U.S.C. § 7714

remediation.title: Supervening illegality — mistake vs impracticability
remediation.signal: A federal criminal statute takes effect between offer and acceptance, unknown to both parties, and the contract performance has become illegal.
remediation.studentMove: Resolve formation first (revocation needs receipt; rejection needs receipt; acceptance is dispatch). Then apply the Gold Key: the NCBE framed key is mutual mistake; impracticability is co-credited.
remediation.tinyRule: When a supervening criminal statute triggers, both mutual mistake and supervening impracticability may discharge; the NCBE's framed key is mutual mistake.
remediation.trap: The dominant trap is the most-picked answer (impracticability). It is doctrinally true; the discrimination is which framing the NCBE key picks.
